title: Collections
summary: List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue and Stack: their costs, TryGetValue versus the indexer, key comparers, modifying a list while iterating, read-only views, and choosing the right collection.
lesson:
## The everyday collections

| type | strength | lookup cost |
|---|---|---|
| `List<T>` | ordered, indexable, growable array | by index O(1), by value O(n) |
| `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` | lookup by key | O(1) average |
| `HashSet<T>` | unique values, membership | O(1) average |
| `Queue<T>` / `Stack<T>` | FIFO / LIFO work lists | O(1) enqueue / push |
| `SortedDictionary` / `SortedSet` | keys kept in sorted order | O(log n) |

Choosing the right one is most of the performance work in CRUD code: a `List.Contains` inside a loop over 10,000 items is 100 million comparisons; a `HashSet.Contains` is 10,000.

## Dictionary: indexer, Add and TryGetValue

```csharp
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["pen"] = 4 };
stock["ink"]                       // KeyNotFoundException
stock.TryGetValue("ink", out var n)  // false, n = 0: the no-exception lookup
stock["pen"] = 9;                  // indexer SET: adds or overwrites
stock.Add("pen", 1);               // ArgumentException: key already exists
stock.GetValueOrDefault("ink")     // 0
```

Use `TryGetValue` for "may be missing" lookups (one hash lookup instead of `ContainsKey` plus the indexer). Do not rely on Dictionary enumeration order; it is not guaranteed.

`TryAdd` is the non-throwing `Add`: it returns `false` and keeps the existing value. `GetValueOrDefault` returns the type's default, so for an `int` value it cannot tell a stored 0 from a missing key; use `TryGetValue` when that difference matters. On order: entries currently come back in insertion order only until a removal frees a slot, which the next `Add` fills.

## Key equality and comparers

Dictionary and HashSet compare keys with the key type's `Equals` and `GetHashCode` (topic 13). For strings you usually want a comparer:

```csharp
var byEmail = new Dictionary<string, User>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
byEmail["Ana@Example.com"] = ana;
byEmail.ContainsKey("ana@example.com")   // true
```

Never mutate an object that is used as a key: its hash changes and the dictionary can no longer find it.

## Modifying while iterating

```csharp
foreach (var x in list) if (x == 2) list.Remove(x);   // InvalidOperationException: collection was modified
list.RemoveAll(x => x == 2);                           // correct
```

Alternatives: iterate a copy (`foreach (var x in list.ToList())`), loop backwards by index, or build a new list.

The check works through a version number: every `Add`, `Remove` or `Clear` on a `List<T>` bumps it, and the enumerator compares it on each step, so even removing the very last item fails on the next `MoveNext`. Looping backwards by index is safe because a removal only shifts the items after it, which the loop has already visited. A `Dictionary` is more lenient: since .NET Core 3.0, `Remove` during its `foreach` is allowed, while an `Add` still throws.

## Exposing collections

Return `IReadOnlyList<T>` / `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` / `IReadOnlyDictionary` from APIs so callers cannot add or remove. Note this is a read-only **view**: if the owner changes the underlying list, the view reflects it. For a true snapshot, copy (`ToList()`, or the immutable collections in `System.Collections.Immutable`).

## Other details worth knowing

- `list[i]` outside the range throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `HashSet.Add` returns `false` when the value was already present: a cheap "seen before?" check.
- `List<T>` grows by doubling its capacity; pre-size with `new List<T>(count)` when you know the size.
- None of these collections are thread-safe for writes. Use `ConcurrentDictionary` (or a lock) when several threads write.

quiz.prompt: What does `dict["missing"]` do on a Dictionary without that key?
choices: Adds the key with a default value
quiz.explanation: The indexer getter has no value to give back for an absent key, and returning default(TValue) would make a stored 0 or null look the same as "missing", so it throws KeyNotFoundException. Only the indexer setter adds keys; a read never does. ArgumentNullException is reserved for a null key. For lookups that may miss, use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault.

quiz.prompt: What does `dict.Add("pen", 1)` do when "pen" already exists?
choices: Returns false and keeps the old value
quiz.explanation: Add means "insert a new key", so a duplicate is treated as a bug in the caller: Add throws, and the message names the key. It never overwrites; that is the job of the indexer setter, `dict["pen"] = 1`. The non-throwing variant is TryAdd, which returns false and keeps the old value, while Add itself returns nothing.

quiz.prompt: Removing items from a List inside a foreach over that same list...
quiz.explanation: List<T> keeps a version number that every Add or Remove increments, and its enumerator compares that number on each MoveNext. After the first Remove, the next step of the foreach sees a changed version and throws with "Collection was modified". It never silently skips items, and no index goes out of range. Use RemoveAll(predicate), loop backwards by index, or iterate a copy made with ToList().

HashSet<T>.Add returns a bool that reports whether the value was inserted. The set already holds 1 from the collection initialiser, so the second add finds an equal element, leaves the set unchanged and reports that. A duplicate is not an error, so nothing throws, and Add returns a flag rather than the element, so the result is never 1.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a string-keyed Dictionary match keys case-insensitively?
choices: Calling ToLower() on each key when it is looked up
Using a SortedDictionary, which compares keys ignoring case
Nothing: string keys compare ignoring case by default
quiz.explanation: A Dictionary hashes and compares keys through its IEqualityComparer, and the default one for string is case-sensitive. A comparer passed to the constructor replaces both the hash code and the equality test, so "Pen" and "pen" land on one entry. Lower-casing only at lookup misses keys stored in another case, and a SortedDictionary sorts with a case-sensitive comparer by default.

quiz.prompt: You check 10,000 ids against a list of 10,000 allowed ids. What is the better data structure for the allowed ids?
quiz.explanation: Each lookup in a HashSet<int> hashes the id and checks one bucket, so 10,000 checks cost about 10,000 steps. List.Contains compares against the elements one by one, up to 10,000 per check, which is up to 100 million comparisons in total. A Queue or a LinkedList searches linearly as well and adds nothing for membership. Build the set once, outside the loop.

quiz.prompt: A method returns its private list as `IReadOnlyList<T>`. The class then adds an item. What does a caller holding the view see?
choices: The old count: the view is a snapshot copy
An InvalidOperationException on the next read
The new item: the view shares the same list
The new item once AsReadOnly() is called again
quiz.explanation: Returning a List<T> as IReadOnlyList<T> is only a conversion: the caller holds a reference to the very same list, with the writing members hidden by the interface type. When the class adds an item, the caller's next Count or loop sees it. Nothing is copied, a read never throws, and AsReadOnly is a wrapper over the same list too. For a snapshot, return a copy such as ToList().

quiz.prompt: Is the enumeration order of a Dictionary<TKey, TValue> guaranteed?
choices: Yes: it always follows insertion order
Yes: it is sorted by the keys' hash codes
No: it is shuffled randomly on each enumeration
No: it is an implementation detail
quiz.explanation: The documentation leaves the order of a Dictionary undefined. The current implementation stores entries in an array in insertion order, so small tests often look ordered, but a removal frees a slot that the next Add reuses, and the order changes. It is not sorted by hash code, and it is not reshuffled per enumeration either. Use SortedDictionary, or sort with OrderBy, when order matters.

quiz.prompt: Why is `TryGetValue` preferred over `ContainsKey` followed by the indexer?
choices: It does one hash lookup instead of two
It takes a lock, so it is thread-safe
It caches the value for later lookups
quiz.explanation: ContainsKey hashes the key and searches its bucket, and the indexer then repeats exactly that work to fetch the value. TryGetValue searches once and hands back both the answer and the value through an out parameter. Neither method allocates or caches anything, and neither makes the dictionary thread-safe, so those are not the reason. A miss simply returns false instead of throwing.

quiz.prompt: Several request threads add to the same Dictionary. What should you use?
quiz.explanation: Dictionary assumes one writer at a time. Two threads inserting at once can both resize the bucket array or link entries into the same chain, which corrupts its internal state: entries go missing, or later calls fail. readonly only stops the field from being reassigned, a List of pairs has the same problem, and [ThreadStatic] gives each thread its own dictionary, so the threads no longer share the data.

flashcards.back: The indexer throws KeyNotFoundException for a missing key; TryGetValue returns false and sets the out value to default.
Add throws when the key exists; assigning through the indexer adds or overwrites.

flashcards.front: How do you remove items while iterating a List?
flashcards.back: Use RemoveAll with a predicate, iterate a copy, or walk the indexes backwards.

flashcards.front: What does HashSet.Add's return value tell you?
flashcards.back: Whether the value was new; false means it was already in the set.

flashcards.front: How do you make string keys case-insensitive?
flashcards.back: Construct the Dictionary or HashSet with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.
No, it is a read-only view; changes by the owner show through. Copy it for a snapshot.

flashcards.front: Why never mutate a dictionary key object?
flashcards.back: Its hash code changes, so the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can no longer be found.

flashcards.front: Which collections are safe for concurrent writes?
flashcards.back: The System.Collections.Concurrent types such as ConcurrentDictionary; the ordinary collections need a lock.

drills.title: Index posts by tag
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The tag page searches every post for every request. Build an index once: tag to posts, case-insensitive, no duplicates."

**Why it matters.** Turning an O(n) scan per request into one O(1) lookup is the most common collection optimisation in CRUD apps, and getting key equality right (case, duplicates) is where it usually goes wrong.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function `Dictionary<string, List<int>> IndexByTag(IEnumerable<Post> posts)`:
- keys are tags, compared case-insensitively (ordinal), so lookups of `"csharp"` and `"CSharp"` find the same entry
- each value is the list of post ids having that tag, in the order the posts appear
- a post lists each of its tags at most once in a tag's list, even if the post repeats the tag in different cases
- blank or whitespace-only tags are ignored; tags are trimmed

**Worked example.** Posts 1 (`"CSharp"`, `"linq"`) and 2 (`"csharp"`) give `csharp → [1, 2]` and `linq → [1]`.
hints: The dictionary itself can be told how to compare keys, and HashSet.Add tells you whether a tag was already seen.

Make both the index and a per-post set of tags already seen compare case-insensitively, normalise each tag before using it, skip blanks and repeats, and create a tag's list the first time you meet the tag.
Build one case-insensitive map from tag to a list of ids, and for every post keep a small case-insensitive set of the tags already handled so a repeated or blank tag is skipped.

drills.title: Bug hunt: index posts by tag
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "Index posts by tag". It compiles and passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec of the local function `Dictionary<string, List<int>> IndexByTag(IEnumerable<Post> posts)` is unchanged:
- keys are tags, compared case-insensitively (ordinal), so lookups of `"csharp"` and `"CSharp"` find the same entry
- each value is the list of post ids having that tag, in the order the posts appear
- a post lists each of its tags at most once in a tag's list, even if the post repeats the tag in different cases
- blank or whitespace-only tags are ignored; tags are trimmed
drills.explanation:
Without a comparer the dictionary compares keys exactly, so `CSharp` and `csharp` become two entries. The test "tags map to post ids in order" then finds only post 2 under `csharp`, and "lookups are case-insensitive" finds nothing for `ef core`. The per-post `seen` set already ignores case, which is why the repeated-tag test passes and hides the problem. Pass the same comparer to the dictionary:

```csharp
var index = new Dictionary<string, List<int>>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
```

Lower-casing each tag before storing it is not enough: the tests also look keys up in upper case, so "lookups are case-insensitive" still fails.
hints: Index two posts tagged with the same tag in different letter cases and count the keys.
The set that dedupes tags inside one post already ignores case, but the index itself does not.
Give the index dictionary the same case-insensitive ordinal comparer as the seen set.
